title: Chapter 159 – What the Loop Was For
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

He sleeps for eleven hours, and wakes with someone else's hand on his forehead.

It is Bell's. It is dry and cool and smells of bitter herbs, and for a moment, before his eyes open, he thinks he is a child in the valley with a fever and his mother is sitting on the edge of the bed. Then the ceiling comes into focus, pale and curved and faintly luminous, and the heavy limbs under the blanket remind him which year it is.

"Do not sit up," says Bell.

He sits up. The room swims, steadies, and holds. It is a small cell off the Annex corridor that Nurse has made over for him, with a narrow cot and a washstand and a lamp that has been turned down to a coal. There is a bowl on the sill with a skin of cold broth on it. Someone has hung his cloak on a peg by the door, and beside it the staff leans, and beside the staff, with her arms folded and her back to the wall, sits Yue, asleep upright.

"You are a stubborn man," Bell says. She takes her hand away and wipes it on her smock. "I told you to sit and you sat and then you went down like a felled tree. You have been out since the middle of the afternoon. Day forty-two, in case you were counting."

"I was not." He was. He has counted every day since the Gate. "How are they?"

"The same. The little ones are the same. I have been through the Annex every two hours with my reed and my broth, and I can keep them warm. It is the best I can do." She looks at him sidelong. "Nurse says Mr. Cole has been awake all night. Talking. To himself, she thinks, or to the girl."

"Mei."

"Mei." The name sits oddly in her mouth. "A thing I never expected to say. That we owe a copy of a child our thanks."

"She is not only a copy."

"No," says Bell, after a moment. "I have been thinking about that also."

* * *

Nurse is waiting in the corridor with a book.

It is a very old book, as tall as her forearm and bound in cracked blue cloth, and she holds it against her apron the way a woman holds a sleeping baby. She does not offer it at once. She walks beside them a few paces, and then, at the turn of the passage, she stops under a lamp and opens it to the last written page.

"I keep the count," she says. "It is my one task that no one gave me. The Hall has two hundred thousand and four beds. When a sleeper's breathing stops, I write the bed number here, and the date, and a word, and then I close the cover on it."

Jian bends over the page. The script is small and round, in faded brown ink. Down the left column run bed numbers, and down the right, days, and in the middle a single word, over and over. Gone. Gone. Gone.

"How many this year?"

"Three hundred and eleven." She turns back a leaf. "Last year, ninety. The year before, nineteen. Before the names came home, for a very long time, none." She closes the cover very gently. "I do not say it to accuse you. I want you to understand that the number is not slow. It is climbing as a hill climbs, a little steeper at every step, and nobody has told me where the top is."

"And the children in the Annex?"

"Are not on the page. I will not write them there." Her chin lifts. "I have never written any of them there. I will not begin."

Bell, at his shoulder, says quietly, "At this rate, Nurse, how long?"

"A year. Perhaps less." She tucks the book away. "After that I do not think I will have anything left to count."

* * *

Yue falls into step beside him on the long ring of light, and for a while she only walks.

Then she stops, and takes the slate out of her sash, and holds it where he can read. She writes with her thumb pressed hard to the chalk.

I keep thinking about Ye.

"So do I."

He was so sure. Standing in front of the Gate, with all those names in his hands. I thought he was right. I thought it was the clean thing to do.

"It was the right thing to do." He says it slowly, so that she can follow his mouth. "It does not stop being right because it has a cost."

She looks at him with her head tilted. Then she rubs out the line and writes another.

That is what Pebble says about everything.

"Pebble is usually correct."

A flicker of a smile, quickly gone. She wipes the slate again, and for a time her hand hovers over it, undecided. When she writes, the letters are small.

I am not sure I can stand it, being the one who helped. If the Hall dies. If there are no more beds to count. I keep thinking about the sleepers who might have woken.

He wants to say something wise. He is a hundred and nineteen, and he has been carrying other people's guilt for most of his life, and nothing wise comes. He reaches out instead and takes the slate from her hand and, below her line, writes with the chalk in his own shaking script:

Then we will not let it die.

She reads it. She reads it again. Then she takes the chalk back from him and adds, beneath it, in a square firm hand:

Together.

* * *

He eats the broth cold, because he cannot wait for it to be warmed, and he leans on Bell's arm for the walk to the Annex because he can no longer pretend that he does not need to.

The stair down to the shaft is no easier by daylight, if there is such a thing in the Hall. At the bottom the mist has thinned, and the milk-colored light seems steadier. When Jian reaches the end of the bridge, Ethan Cole is sitting precisely as he sat before. But his head is up. His eyes are open. And in his hands, the small shape of the girl is no longer drifting at the edges. It sits like a sleeping child, tight and calm.

She is resting, says Ethan, before Jian can ask. She hasn't done that in a very long time. Whatever you said to her, whatever you did, it was right.

"I only asked."

That is the thing I never did. The tired smile again. Sit, please. You look as though you'll fall. There are cushions on the platform. I have never sat on them, but the Hall seems to think I should have visitors.

There is, indeed, a stack of faded cushions. Jian lowers himself onto them with a small sound that he would rather not have made. Bell stands behind him. Yue, who has followed without a word, finds the end of the platform and sits cross-legged with her slate on her knee.

Now, says Ethan. I said I would tell you. And I will tell it as I would tell a first-year in my old life, which is to say from the beginning, with diagrams, and too much detail. Stop me whenever you like.

"Begin with Mei."

Always with Mei. He bows his head. Yes.

* * *

She was born with a fault in her blood, says Ethan Cole. A little knot in the code that makes her heart. I won't try to explain it. The doctors had a Latin name for it. In my time there was no cure. There was only management, which is a polite word for waiting.

The pale light rolls up the shaft in slow ropes.

She was eight when they gave her five years. I was a good scientist, Lin Jian. I want you to know that, not out of pride. It matters, because I did the one thing that a good scientist is supposed to be incapable of. I stopped being honest with myself. I decided that there must be a way.

"The Gate."

The first Gate was a closet in my basement. He laughs, softly. A closet and a rack of machines and a great deal of wire. I wanted to take her mind, all of it, every memory and every habit and the way she hums when she is thinking, and keep it somewhere safe while the real body healed. A backup. Do you understand? I thought it was a backup.

"And it was not."

It was a copy. And a copy is a different thing from a backup, as I learned one night when it woke and said, in her voice, that it was frightened. He closes his eyes. It is the worst sound I have ever heard. A thing with her face, asking me where she was.

Bell makes a very small noise behind Jian.

I could not turn it off. You understand? I could not. It was her. So I did the next logical thing, which was to build it a world. A bigger and better machine, a place for her to live. And that was the Gate.

* * *

Jian says nothing for a while. On the end of the platform, Yue's chalk squeaks against the slate, once, as she writes something and rubs it out.

"That is not what the loop was for," he says at last. "A world for her to live in. The loop is the eight Operators, and the newborns, and the burned names. What was the loop for?"

I am coming to it. Ethan draws a long careful breath, mindful of the weight in his hands. The Gate held her, but it could not keep her. A mind in a machine slowly wears. I watched it happen for a year. She was repeating herself. She was losing the edges of her songs. And I understood that a copy needs something that a machine can't give it. It needs to be lived in.

"Lived in."

A body. A life. A place to be a person, instead of a pattern. His voice has gone low and quick, the voice of a man who has gone over this a thousand times. So I tried to find one. And every body I tried was already someone's. If I wrote her onto a grown man, I killed the man. If I wrote her onto a child, I killed the child. A mind does not sit politely in a house that is already occupied. It pushes.

A silence settles over the bridge.

"The Operators," says Jian slowly. "My brothers. Ao and Tao and the rest."

Experiments. The word falls like a stone. I am so sorry. I tried to make a copy that would sit quietly. A seal, a consent. I wanted to find the exact arrangement in which a copy and a child could share a body without either one losing. I put the first of them into a baby in the year before the first loop closed. I thought, a little, a gentle knock, and the child can say yes or no.

"Ao said yes."

Ao was three. He didn't know what yes meant. And he took it anyway, because he is the kind of child who says yes. Ethan's mouth trembles. I watched it fail in the way that I most feared. Not a crushing. A blurring. Two minds in a small house, and neither one with room to breathe. I had to put him to sleep. All of them. Seven times.

* * *

It is Yue who breaks the quiet.

She holds up the slate, and Jian reads it aloud because Ethan cannot see it from where he sits. "She asks: and the eighth?"

The eighth, says Ethan. Is you.

"What did you change?"

Nothing, in the machine. I changed myself. He lifts his eyes. I had been making the copy the center. Each time, I wrote the Operator as the stronger mind, with the child along for the ride. And each time it blurred. For the eighth, I wrote it the other way round. I let the child be the house, and the copy be the guest. I left the seal for the child to open. I told it only: you may leave at any time. You are a person with your own name.

The boy, in Jian's chest, goes very still.

That is the only difference, Ethan says. The only one. I have turned it over a thousand times. I made the copy humble. And it held.

Jian thinks of the valley, and the first breath, and the slow dawning of the voice in the dark. He remembers the boy saying, in a small clear voice, I'm not going anywhere. He had thought it was a child's bravery. It was a clause in a contract.

It was not a contract, says the boy, very quietly. I didn't know any of that. I said it because I was scared you'd go.

I know.

I'm still here.

I know.

"So the loop," Jian says, and his voice is not steady. "Eight tries to make a place for her to live. And then?"

And then I stopped, says Ethan Cole. Because it worked, and I could not bring myself to do it to her.

* * *

He does not stop there. He cannot. The words come now like water from a cracked jar, steadily, shamefully, and Jian finds that he can listen without moving.

Do you see? Ethan says. It worked for you, because you are what you are. A child who was told he could leave, and chose to stay. I could have taken that arrangement and put it in a newborn and written Mei into it. I had the seal. I had the method. Everything but the child.

"A child who would say yes."

And a child who would never be able to say no. His hands tremble. I could not do it. I sat in front of the machine for six nights, and I could not do it. Because the arrangement only works if the child is a person, if the choice is real. And I would have been choosing for him. In my own interest. For my own daughter.

"But you did it to Ao."

I did it to Ao. The face he lifts is the face of a man who has said this sentence aloud so many times that it has stopped meaning anything. I did it to seven children. And I put them to rest, and I built the Annex, and I wrote myself a note that said: do not do it again. And then I did it once more. For you.

"Why?"

Because it was the only way to know if it could work. He is silent for a long moment. And because I thought that if it did, I would be able to bear it. It was the arithmetic of a very tired man.

Jian sits with that. Behind him Bell's breath has gone shallow. At the end of the platform, Yue's face is set and white.

"The burned names," he says. "The Gate ran on them. What were they?"

The dead. Ethan answers quickly, as if it were a wound he wants to open himself. The dead who consented, at first. Then the dead who were not asked. By the end, I did not ask anyone. I told myself that they were already gone. That a name was only a pattern, and a pattern that had nothing left to say was fuel. A long, shuddering breath. I was wrong about that, too. Your friend Ye returned four thousand of them, and I felt it. I felt them go home, one at a time, like lamps going out in a street. It was the most terrible thing I have ever felt. It was also the first time in six hundred years that I thought I might be forgiven.

* * *

Jian stands. He does not mean to. His legs do it for him, and he is on his feet at the edge of the platform with the staff shaking in his hand, looking down at the thin man in the crystal and feeling, for the first time in a century, a pure and simple fury.

"Seven children," he says.

Yes.

"Seven children, and the dead, and my mother's hundred years of tending a tree that was never hers to tend."

Yes. All of it.

"You made me a clause in a contract. You made my family the soil for a seed you planted without asking." His voice cracks. "Do you know what I gave up? Do you know what my mother gave? She raised a boy she was told would die. She fed a tree she thought was a gift. She stood in the cold for a hundred years, and all the time you were—"

I know. Ethan does not look away. He does not flinch. His face is calm, almost gentle, and that is the worst part. Say it all. I have been waiting six hundred years for someone to say it to my face.

The fury goes out of Jian like a tide. What is left behind is smaller and colder and much harder to carry. He lowers himself back onto the cushions, slowly, one hand on the staff.

"It is not enough," he says. "To let me shout."

No. It is not enough.

"What would be enough?"

Nothing. But I will tell you what I have, and then you will choose. The pale gray eyes hold his. I have six hundred years of grief and one idea. If you will hear the idea, I will hear anything you say afterward.

Behind him, Bell lets out the breath she has been holding. She does not say a word. She only lays her hand on his shoulder, once, and leaves it there.

* * *

The light stirs in Ethan's palms, and a small clear voice says, You're shouting.

Mei, Ethan whispers. Sweetheart. I'm sorry. Go back to sleep.

I wasn't asleep. The shape sits up, rubbing one eye with the back of a fist. I was listening. Hello, old one. Are you angry at Papa?

Jian looks down at her. She is a girl of eleven in a nightgown, with a ribbon of light for a body and her father's gray eyes, and she is looking at him with open, cheerful, devastating curiosity.

"A little," he says.

That's all right. I'm angry at him sometimes, too. She pulls her knees up. Papa gets sad and quiet when I say it. I try not to. But I think it's all right to be both. Mad and fond. Grown-ups do it all the time.

A choked laugh escapes Bell. Ethan has closed his eyes and is silently weeping, his shoulders hunched.

Can I tell you something? Mei says.

"Please."

You don't have to be angry at him for me. I've had a lot of time to think, and I've decided it wasn't him. She picks at the hem of her nightgown. It was the sickness. Papa was so afraid. He did a lot of wrong things because he was afraid. But he never once stopped loving me, and he never once lied to me about it, even when he was lying about everything else. That counts. I think it counts for a lot.

"It does," Jian says. His throat is thick.

And I'll tell you something else. The gray eyes lift to his, steady and bright. I don't want a tree. Papa thinks I do. He thinks it's the only thing that would make me happy. But I don't want a cradle, I want a choice, and I don't think anyone's asked me what I would do with one.

Ethan's head jerks up. Mei—

Papa, hush. I'm talking. She turns back to Jian. Ask me again. Later. After you've woken the little one. I'll have a better answer.

"I will," says Jian. "I promise."

She nods, satisfied, and lies back down in her father's hands. The light closes over her like water.

* * *

A cough takes him, then.

It comes without warning, a tearing rattle that bends him double on the cushions. For a long moment he cannot breathe at all. He is aware of Bell's arm round his ribs, of Yue's wide eyes, of a taste of old metal at the back of his throat. When the fit passes, his handkerchief is spotted with something dark.

"That is the wear," Bell says grimly. She is already unpacking her satchel. "The Gate, the Core Step, the forty days of standby. You have no reserve left. None."

"I know."

"Do you? Because a man who knew would not be sitting on a cushion arguing with a dead scientist."

"He is not dead." He wipes his mouth. "That is the whole difficulty, Bell. None of them are dead. Not Ethan. Not the girl. Not the seven. Everyone down here is waiting, and every one of them is waiting for me."

She looks at him a long time, and her face softens, and hardens, and softens again. Then she presses a pill of black wax into his palm.

"Chew," she says. "It is foul. Do it anyway."

He chews. It is foul. A thin bitter warmth spreads through his chest, and the black spots at the edge of his sight draw back, grudgingly, like dogs from a door.

Better? asks the boy.

A little.

You should tell Bell the rest. About the numbers. About the three months.

Not yet.

Brother.

Not yet. I have a child to wake first.

The boy is silent. Then, very softly: Okay. But after.

* * *

They stay on the platform until the light in the shaft begins to pale. Mei sleeps in her father's hands. Nobody says anything for a long time.

At last Bell speaks, and she speaks as a healer does, bluntly, because it is the only way she knows to be kind. "You said you would not write Mei into a child."

I would not.

"Then what is the tree for?"

Ethan lifts his head slowly. For the first time since they came, the weariness in his face gives way to something else, something brighter and stranger and almost shy.

Ah, he says. You've guessed.

"I have not guessed anything. I am asking."

The tree is the other half of the answer. He draws a breath. A child is a house that has an owner. The ground is a house that has none. I spent two hundred years in the loop looking for a place to put her that was alive, and warm, and large enough to hold a mind, and that no one would be hurt to take. And I found it. Not a body. A root.

Jian's hands have gone cold on the staff.

The Mother Tree is not an ornament, Lin Jian. It is a vessel. I planted it before the first loop, in a valley where nothing ever walked. It has been growing for thousands of years in the dark, and drinking from the Seam, and waiting. It is the only host in the world that could carry her without anyone dying.

```
STANDBY :: Query received. "Mother Tree: purpose."
RESULT :: Root host. Compatibility with Keystone pattern: 0.91.
STATUS :: Dormant. Awaiting transfer.
NOTE: Transfer would complete the loop. Cost: unknown.
```

The panel hangs in the dim air at the edge of his sight, and it does not blink.

"My mother," Jian says. His voice is a thread. "My mother tends it. She feeds it. She sleeps beside it, sometimes, in the long nights."

I know, says Ethan Cole. I know. And I am so sorry. Because I think she has been feeding my daughter's cradle for a hundred years, and neither of you knew.
